extracted.intended_audience: British political class, legislators, and educated public debating the implications of the French Revolution (late 18th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative principles and legal-political standards about the legitimacy of sovereigns, limits of revolutionary claims (right to elect or cashier governors), and the proper constitutional means of change in the British polity.

rubrics_metrics.name: No general right 'to choose our own governors' from 1688
rubrics_metrics.description: The Declaration of Right (act of 1 William and Mary) contains no suggestion of a general right 'to choose our own governors,' 'to cashier them for misconduct,' or 'to frame a government for ourselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the text of the Declaration of Right as the authoritative source for the principles of the 1688 Revolution; do not infer a broad elective right where the statute is silent. Anti-pattern: treating the Revolution as having created an abstract popular right to elect sovereigns rather than as having settled succession and rights together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights and succession are indissolubly connected in the Declaration of Right
rubrics_metrics.description: The Declaration of Right declares rights and the settlement of the succession 'in one body, and bound indissolubly together.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret constitutional acts as integrating protections of rights with the form of succession chosen; one should not separate the two to claim a new principle of elective sovereignty. Example: reading the statute as endorsing elective monarchy is a misreading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty in succession is necessary for unity, peace, and tranquillity
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislature declared that 'a certainty in the succession thereof the unity, peace, and tranquillity of this nation doth, under God, wholly depend.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize legal and predictable rules of succession to preserve national stability. Anti-pattern: adopting claims or practices that create uncertainty in succession because they risk civil disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary succession as the constitutional means to secure liberties
rubrics_metrics.description: The hereditary crown, continued by law and statute, is presented as the course by which liberties can be 'regularly perpetuated and preserved sacred as our hereditary right.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value continuity of hereditary succession as a constitutional safeguard for other institutions and liberties; prefer preserving an inheritable line to introducing elective principles that might unsettle laws and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary exceptions do not become general principles (privilegium non transit in exemplum)
rubrics_metrics.description: A law made in a special case (an act of necessity) should not be generalized into a principle applicable in all cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing precedents arising from exceptional circumstances (e.g., the Revolution's temporary deviations), do not extrapolate them into universal constitutional doctrines. Anti-pattern: converting emergency measures into permanent constitutional rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislature may exercise broad abstract competence but is morally constrained
rubrics_metrics.description: While the supreme power may have abstract competence to do many things, there are intelligible 'moral' limits subjecting such will to reason, faith, justice, and fixed fundamental policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess legislative actions not only by bare power but by whether they respect enduring principles of justice and constitutional faith. Example: even if Parliament could technically do something extreme, morally it should refrain when it would decompose the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constituent parts cannot renounce essential public faith and obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Constituent parts of the state (e.g., House of Lords, House of Commons) are obliged to hold their public faith with each other and cannot morally abdicate their portion of authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid legal or political moves that would amount to one part of the constitution surrendering its essential role or betraying public trust. Anti-pattern: proposing that the Lords dissolve itself or the Commons renounce its authority as legitimate constitutional acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Revolution did not create a right to elect sovereigns; Parliament renounced any such right
rubrics_metrics.description: So far from acquiring a right to elect kings by the Revolution, the nation at that time 'most solemnly renounce[d] and abdicate[d] it, for themselves, and for all their posterity forever.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat historical legislative language and pledges as binding evidence of constitutional intent. Do not claim revolutionary authority where Parliament explicitly entrenched hereditary succession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deriving present law from confused conflation of different revolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not conflate the Revolution of 1688 with earlier English upheavals or the French Revolution; examine the actual acts (statutes) to discover principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting revolutionary precedent, distinguish among distinct events and consult the actual statutes and their contexts rather than rhetorical analogies. Anti-pattern: using the French Revolution as an immediate template for English constitutional claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impeachment, frequent parliaments, and legal safeguards preferable to 'cashiering' sovereigns
rubrics_metrics.description: The framers of the Declaration of Right and the limitation acts secured liberties by making ministers responsible, ensuring frequent meetings of Parliament, and providing for impeachment rather than endorsing a vague right to depose monarchs for 'misconduct.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer institutional, legal mechanisms of accountability (parliamentary oversight, impeachment) as constitutional remedies for misconduct rather than recourse to popular deposition. Example: the statute forbidding pardon under the great seal to be pleadable against an impeachment strengthens parliamentary control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of a sovereign by force (cashiering) is a case of war, not of constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: The ceremony of cashiering kings usually requires force and becomes a case of war, where laws and tribunals fall silent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that violent or extralegal removal undermines legal order and produces civil war conditions; constitutional change should avoid methods that reduce disputes to arms.

rubrics_metrics.name: The king is not a servant in the ordinary legal sense and is not removable at pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Although kings are said to be servants of the public in a rhetorical sense, under the Constitution the king 'obey[s] no other person' and is not a servant whose situation is to obey commands or be removable at will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not legislate or argue as if the sovereign were subject to ordinary servant-like accountability; analyze the king's role under law as a distinct, high-magistrate office. Anti-pattern: adopting rhetoric that implies direct popular control and removal of the monarch as if he were an ordinary officer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating elective title as sole lawful title invalidates past laws and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: If once established that no throne is lawful but the elective, then acts done under prior sovereigns would be exposed as invalid, risking the annulment of essential statutes (e.g., Habeas Corpus, Petition of Right).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware constitutional doctrines that, if applied retroactively or absolutely, would cast doubt on the continuity and validity of the existing body of statute law and rights. Anti-pattern: using abstract principles that undermine the legal continuity of the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for preserving old constitutional parts and regenerating deficient parts
rubrics_metrics.description: In times of crisis the polity should regenerate the deficient part of the old Constitution through the parts not impaired, keeping old parts unchanged so the recovered part fits with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reforming, confine change to the defective element and preserve the established framework to maintain coherence. Example: at the Restoration and the Revolution, England repaired parts without decomposing the whole system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative acts creating succession can bind heirs and posterity
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of the 12th and 13th of King William binds 'us, and our heirs, and our posterity, to them, their heirs, and their posterity' (the Protestant line), thereby securing both an hereditary crown and an hereditary allegiance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that parliamentary settlement of succession can create long-lasting legal limitations and that such enactments are intended to secure continuity. Use statutory language to assess the intended permanence of constitutional arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using equivocations and slippery constructions to disguise abstract principles
rubrics_metrics.description: When revolutionaries assert the king 'owes his crown to the choice of his people,' they may later equivocate to reduced meanings (e.g., ‘some predecessors chosen’) to make the proposition nugatory; such subterfuges conceal the true principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize ambiguous or evasive formulations and insist on the plain meaning and practical tendency of doctrines. Anti-pattern: accepting strained interpretations that neutralize clear political doctrines while introducing latent principles for future use.
